claim: Several ganglion cell types in the macaque monkey retina show selectivity to approaching motion.
source: Here, we report that detection of approaching motion begins in the retina. Several ganglion cell types, the retinal output neurons, show selectivity to approaching motion.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings from multiple ganglion cell types showing differential responses to approaching vs. receding motion stimuli.

claim: The preference for approaching motion arises in the interplay between presynaptic excitatory and inhibitory circuit elements.
source: Synaptic current recordings from these cells further reveal that this preference for approaching motion arises in the interplay between presynaptic excitatory and inhibitory circuit elements.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents showing differential patterns for approaching vs. receding motion.

claim: The elementary computations that detect approaching motion begin early in the visual stream of primates.
source: Moreover, the elementary computations that detect approaching motion begin early in the visual stream of primates.
evidence: Based on recordings from retinal ganglion cells, which are the earliest output neurons in the primate visual pathway.

claim: Many animals use size changes on the retina to estimate whether and when an object will collide with the animal.
source: Many animals use these size changes to estimate whether and when an object will collide with the animal (Schiff and Detwiler, 1979; Lee, 1976; Kaiser and Hecht, 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on collision detection.

claim: Animals use size changes on the retina to estimate their own motion through the environment.
source: Many animals use these size changes to estimate whether and when an object will collide with the animal (Schiff and Detwiler, 1979; Lee, 1976; Kaiser and Hecht, 1995) and also to estimate the animal's own motion through the environment (Clifford et al., 1999; Schrater et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on self-motion estimation.

claim: Neurons with selectivity for approaching motion have been found in the dorsal visual pathway of primates.
source: Neurons with such selectivity for approaching motion have been found in the dorsal visual pathway of primates (Orban et al., 1992; Duffy and Wurtz, 1991; Wang and Yao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies identifying approach-selective neurons in primate cortex.

claim: It is not known whether similar approach selectivity is found earlier in the visual pathway of primates.
source: However, it is not known whether similar approach selectivity is found earlier in the visual pathway of primates.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature prior to this study.

claim: Parasol ganglion cells project to the dorsal visual pathway.
source: Several ganglion cell types found in the retinas of humans and non-human primates project to the dorsal visual pathway, including parasol (magnocellular-projecting) cells (Rodieck and Watanabe, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical study.

claim: Parasol cells can detect small changes in the reflectance of an object relative to the background.
source: These cells can detect small changes in the reflectance of an object relative to the background (i.e. contrast)
evidence: Based on established knowledge of parasol cell properties.

claim: The high contrast sensitivity of parasol cells has resulted in the hypothesis that these cells contribute primarily to representations of object form.
source: and their high contrast sensitivity has resulted in the hypothesis that these cells contribute primarily to representations of object form (Kaplan and Shapley, 1986; Lee et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Less is known about how motion affects the response properties of parasol cells.
source: Less is known about how motion affects the response properties of these cells (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2003; Frechette et al., 2005; Manookin et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of limited knowledge in the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Parasol and other ganglion cell types in the macaque monkey retina display a preference for approaching motion.
source: Here, we report that parasol and other ganglion cell types in the macaque monkey retina display a preference for approaching motion.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings showing higher responses to approaching vs. receding stimuli.

claim: Visual circuits downstream of parasol cells can detect approaching motion based solely on the spike output of these cells.
source: We show that visual circuits downstream of parasol cells can detect approaching motion based solely on the spike output of these cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational decoding models applied to model parasol cell outputs.

claim: Five ganglion cell types were recorded: broad thorny, On and Off smooth monostratified, and On and Off parasol ganglion cells.
source: We recorded the spike responses of five ganglion cell types—broad thorny, On and Off smooth monostratified, and On and Off parasol ganglion cells—in an in vitro preparation of the macaque monkey retina
evidence: Description of experimental methods and cell types studied.

claim: Cells were identified based on their characteristic cell body sizes and shapes under infrared illumination, their distinct light response properties, and dendritic morphologies.
source: Cells were identified based on their characteristic cell body sizes and shapes under infrared illumination, their distinct light response properties, and dendritic morphologies (Puller et al., 2015; Watanabe and Rodieck, 1989; Crook et al., 2008; Rhoades et al., 2019; Petrusca et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of cell identification methods with supporting citations.

claim: Humans and non-human primates use changes in spatial scale or object size in estimating the speed of approaching objects.
source: Humans and non-human primates use changes in spatial scale or object size in estimating the speed of approaching objects and their own motion through the environment (Schiff and Detwiler, 1979; Lee, 1976; Kaiser and Hecht, 1995; Clifford et al., 1999; Schrater et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Selectivity for approaching motion is commonly thought to originate in the thalamus or visual cortex of primates.
source: Further, this selectivity for approaching motion is commonly thought to originate in the thalamus or visual cortex of primates (Wang and Yao, 2011)
evidence: Statement of prevailing view in the literature with supporting citation.

claim: A retinal origin for approach motion sensitivity has not been considered in primates.
source: and a retinal origin for this type of motion sensitivity has not been considered.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Approaching textures elicited larger spike responses than receding textures in parasol, smooth monostratified, and broad thorny ganglion cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1, approaching textures elicited larger spike responses than receding textures in parasol, smooth monostratified, and broad thorny (On-Off type) ganglion cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: A large bistratified ganglion cell showed increased spiking to approaching textures, but the bias to approaching motion was not as strong as that observed in the other cell types.
source: A large bistratified ganglion cell–another type of On-Off cell—also showed increased spiking to approaching textures, but the bias to approaching motion was not as strong as that observed in the other cell types (Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Preference for approaching motion is not a universal property of all primate ganglion cells, but is restricted to a subset of these cell types.
source: This finding indicated that preference for approaching motion was not a universal property of all primate ganglion cells, but was restricted to a subset of these cell types.
evidence: Inferred from differential responses across cell types shown in Figure 1.

claim: Approaching textures elicited higher spike rates in On- and Off-type parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells, resulting in significant approach selectivity values in all four cell types.
source: Indeed, the approaching textures elicited higher spike rates in On- and Off-type parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells, resulting in significant approach selectivity values in all four cell types (Figure 1C; p<7.8 × 10–3; Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The smallest texture scales used in the experiments corresponded in size to the dendritic tree diameters of the diffuse bipolar cells that provide excitatory synaptic input to parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells in the mid-peripheral retina (∼30–40 µm).
source: The smallest texture scales used in these experiments corresponded in size to the dendritic tree diameters of the diffuse bipolar cells that provide excitatory synaptic input to parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells in the mid-peripheral retina (∼30–40 µm) (Dacey et al., 2000; Boycott and Wässle, 1991; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2015; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2016; Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: Based on anatomical measurements from cited studies.

claim: Approach selectivity persisted in parasol and smooth monostratified cells across different scale ranges of texture sequences.
source: Approach selectivity persisted in parasol and smooth monostratified cells across these stimulus conditions (parasol: n = 16 cells, p<2.4 × 10–4; smooth monostratified: n = 7 cells, p<7.8 × 10–3; Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings at multiple spatial frequency ranges with statistical analysis.

claim: Approach selectivity increased with increasing texture scale (i.e. decreasing spatial frequency) in both parasol and smooth monostratified cells.
source: In fact, approach selectivity increased with increasing texture scale (i.e. decreasing spatial frequency) in both parasol and smooth monostratified cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings at different spatial frequencies shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mechanisms mediating approach selectivity in parasol and smooth monostratified cells operate across a wide range of spatial scales.
source: These results indicated that the mechanisms mediating approach selectivity in these cells operate across a wide range of spatial scales.
evidence: Inferred from persistence of approach selectivity across different spatial frequency ranges.

claim: The texture stimuli contained similar statistical properties to the types of motion encountered during optical flow.
source: Further, the texture stimuli contained similar statistical properties to the types of motion encountered during optical flow
evidence: Based on stimulus design matching properties of natural optical flow.

claim: Signals from parasol and smooth monostratified cells could be utilized in detecting optical flow motion.
source: indicating that signals from parasol and smooth monostratified cells could be utilized in detecting this type of motion.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of stimulus properties to optical flow and observed approach selectivity.

claim: Neurons in macaque visual cortex show a preference for approaching textures, which is thought to arise from the linear spatiotemporal receptive-field structure of these cells.
source: Neurons in macaque visual cortex show a preference for approaching textures, which is thought to arise from the linear spatiotemporal receptive-field structure of these cells (Wang and Yao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on cortical neurons.

claim: Neural mechanisms operating much earlier in the visual pathway might also contribute to the observed preference for approaching motion.
source: However, neural mechanisms operating much earlier in the visual pathway might also contribute to the observed preference for approaching motion.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential retinal contributions.

claim: The excitatory synaptic output from retinal bipolar cells onto the dendrites of ganglion cells is a strong candidate for contributing to approach motion selectivity.
source: We considered the excitatory synaptic output from retinal bipolar cells onto the dendrites of ganglion cells as a strong candidate for contributing to this type of stimulus selectivity.
evidence: Hypothesis based on known properties of bipolar cell outputs.

claim: The synaptic output of retinal bipolar cells is strongly rectified (nonlinear).
source: The synaptic output of retinal bipolar cells is strongly rectified (nonlinear) (Demb et al., 1999; Schwartz et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on bipolar cell physiology.

claim: Bipolar cell output rectification is critical for detecting certain types of visual motion.
source: and this rectification is critical for detecting certain types of visual motion (Demb et al., 2001; Baccus et al., 2008; Kuo et al., 2016; Manookin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on motion detection.

claim: Subunit receptive-field models were created based on direct measurements of the spatiotemporal filtering properties and output nonlinearities of diffuse bipolar cells in macaque retina.
source: We created subunit receptive-field models based on direct measurements of the spatiotemporal filtering properties and output nonlinearities of the diffuse bipolar cells that provide excitatory synaptic input to parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells in the macaque monkey retina.
evidence: Description of computational modeling approach based on physiological measurements.

claim: The spatial components of the model bipolar cell receptive fields were based on previous measurements of these cells.
source: The spatial components of the model bipolar cell receptive fields were based on previous measurements of these cells (Dacey et al., 2000; Boycott and Wässle, 1991; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2015; Turner and Rieke, 2016)
evidence: Model parameters derived from cited anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: The temporal filtering properties, electrical coupling, and output nonlinearities of model bipolar cells were based on direct measurements.
source: and the temporal filtering properties, electrical coupling, and output nonlinearities were based on our own direct measurements (Manookin et al., 2018).
evidence: Model parameters derived from authors' previous physiological measurements.

claim: The receptive-field profile of ganglion cells was modeled as a difference-of-Gaussians in which the receptive-field center was opposed by a surround of opposite contrast polarity.
source: The receptive-field profile of ganglion cells was modeled as a difference-of-Gaussians in which the receptive-field center was opposed by a surround of opposite contrast polarity.
evidence: Description of computational modeling approach.

claim: The sizes and strengths of the center and surround regions of the receptive field were determined directly by measuring spike responses to sinusoidally modulated spots that varied in diameter.
source: The sizes and strengths of the center and surround regions of the receptive field were determined directly by measuring spike responses to sinusoidally modulated spots that varied in diameter (14–720 µm)—the relative sizes and strengths of center (wC) and surround (wS) regions of the receptive field were estimated from these response patterns (Figure 2B, C; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Model parameters derived from physiological measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both center and surround regions of the model ganglion cell receptive field were comprised of subunits.
source: Both center and surround regions were comprised of subunits
evidence: Description of computational model architecture.

claim: The surround provided lateral inhibition to the model ganglion cell with a temporal delay.
source: and the surround provided lateral inhibition to the model ganglion cell with a temporal delay (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of computational model architecture.

claim: Surround inhibition typically arises via feedback from horizontal cells or amacrine cells and must traverse an extra synapse relative to the direct excitatory synaptic input from bipolar cells.
source: This delay occurs because surround inhibition typically arises via feedback from horizontal cells or amacrine cells and, thus, must traverse an extra synapse relative to the direct excitatory synaptic input from bipolar cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of retinal circuitry.

claim: The surround delay was directly measured by recording responses to spots presented over the receptive-field center or annuli presented in the surround.
source: We directly measured the surround delay by recording responses to spots presented over the receptive-field center or annuli presented in the surround.
evidence: Description of physiological measurement method.

claim: The temporal delay between center and surround regions was determined from the difference in the time-to-peak of the temporal filters measured in the center and surround regions of the receptive field.
source: The temporal delay between center and surround regions was determined from the difference in the time-to-peak of the temporal filters measured in the center and surround regions of the receptive field (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: Description of analysis method with data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: The outputs of the linear subunit model were similar for both approaching and receding textures, resulting in a lack of approach selectivity.
source: The outputs of the linear subunit model were similar for both approaching and receding textures, resulting in a lack of approach selectivity (p>0.4 at all expansion rates; Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nonlinear subunit model showed that approaching textures produced significantly larger outputs than receding textures for each expansion rate.
source: However, the nonlinear subunit model showed a very different pattern—approaching textures produced significantly larger outputs than receding textures for each expansion rate and this bias for approaching motion increased with increasing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The nonlinear output of retinal bipolar cells may contribute to approach selectivity in some ganglion cell types.
source: These modeling results suggest that the nonlinear output of retinal bipolar cells may contribute to approach selectivity in some ganglion cell types (see Appendix 1 for a more detailed treatment of this subject).
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results showing approach selectivity with nonlinear subunits.

claim: Previous studies posited that approach selectivity arose in the cortex or thalamus.
source: Previous studies posited that this type of approach selectivity arose in the cortex or thalamus (Wang and Yao, 2011)
evidence: Statement of previous theoretical view with supporting citation.

claim: Physiological recordings indicated that some primate ganglion cell types showed approach selectivity.
source: Our physiological recordings, however, indicated that some primate ganglion cell types showed approach selectivity.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings from multiple ganglion cell types.

claim: Modeling results indicated that approach sensitivity was predicted as a consequence of ganglion cells pooling across several nonlinear subunits.
source: Moreover, our modeling results indicated that approach sensitivity was predicted as a consequence of ganglion cells pooling across several nonlinear subunits.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: Individual parasol cells could distinguish between approaching or receding texture motion with a high degree of accuracy.
source: Our physiological recordings indicated that individual parasol cells could distinguish between approaching or receding texture motion with a high degree of accuracy (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each subclass of parasol ganglion cell (On or Off) forms a regularly spaced mosaic with neighboring cells of the same class.
source: Each subclass of parasol ganglion cell (On or Off) forms a regularly spaced mosaic with neighboring cells of the same class, but the dendritic-field and receptive-field locations between On and Off types are uncorrelated (Watanabe and Rodieck, 1989; Field et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The dendritic-field and receptive-field locations between On and Off parasol cell types are uncorrelated.
source: Each subclass of parasol ganglion cell (On or Off) forms a regularly spaced mosaic with neighboring cells of the same class, but the dendritic-field and receptive-field locations between On and Off types are uncorrelated (Watanabe and Rodieck, 1989; Field et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The On and Off models showed larger responses for approaching textures relative to their receding counterparts.
source: As with our direct recordings, the On and Off models showed larger responses for approaching textures relative to their receding counterparts (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both linear and quadratic decoding models showed Jensen-Shannon distance values ≥0.28 under all conditions and values near one at the higher speeds tested.
source: Indeed, both decoding models showed Jensen-Shannon distance values ≥0.28 under all conditions and values near one at the higher speeds tested (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Downstream circuits could accurately detect approaching motion with very simple processing of the inputs from On and Off parasol cells.
source: These results indicated that downstream circuits could accurately detect approaching motion with very simple processing of the inputs from On and Off parasol cells.
evidence: Inferred from high decoding accuracy of simple linear and quadratic models.

claim: Increasing the number of model ganglion cell pairs providing input to the linear decoder produced a modest increase in performance.
source: Increasing the number of model ganglion cell pairs providing input to the linear decoder produced a modest increase in performance (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Model performance was high for single ganglion cell pairs, indicating that little integration or post-processing of the retinal output was required to reliably detect approaching motion.
source: However, model performance was high for single ganglion cell pairs, indicating that little integration or post-processing of the retinal output was required to reliably detect approaching motion.
evidence: Inferred from high decoding accuracy with minimal numbers of model cells.

claim: The type of motion studied with the approaching and receding texture stimuli is commonly encountered as an animal moves through the environment.
source: The type of motion that we studied with the approaching and receding texture stimuli is commonly encountered as an animal moves through the environment (Schrater et al., 2001; Dong and Atick, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on natural visual statistics.

claim: The output of the primate retina contains reliable information that could be used by downstream neural pathways for detecting approaching motion.
source: The results presented thus far in our study support the premise that the output of the primate retina contains reliable information that could be used by downstream neural pathways for detecting approaching motion.
evidence: Inferred from physiological recordings and modeling results showing approach selectivity.

claim: The nonlinear subunit model predicted approach selectivity to the expanding texture stimuli but not to the expanding annuli.
source: First, the nonlinear subunit model predicted approach selectivity to the expanding texture stimuli (Figure 3), but not to the expanding annuli.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The linear and nonlinear subunit models both predicted a lack of approach selectivity for the moving annuli.
source: Unlike their predictions for the texture stimuli (Figure 3), the linear and nonlinear subunit models both predicted a lack of approach selectivity for the moving annuli, as model outputs were similar for the approaching and receding annuli at all contrasts (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: The coupled subunit model predicted larger responses to approaching annuli than to receding annuli.
source: The coupled subunit model, however, predicted larger responses to approaching annuli than to receding annuli (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Electrical coupling significantly increases the size of bipolar cell receptive fields according to some studies.
source: Indeed, some studies have proposed that electrical coupling significantly increases the size of bipolar cell receptive fields (Dacey et al., 2000; Kujiraoka and Saito, 1986; Saito and Kujiraoka, 1988), but see Berntson and Taylor (2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, with note of conflicting evidence.

claim: A receptive-field diameter of 32 µm was used in the coupled subunit model based on previous direct measurements.
source: We used a receptive-field diameter of 32 µm in our coupled subunit model that exhibited approach selectivity to moving annuli (two-standard-deviation diameter; Figure 5E). This value was based on a previous study in which we used direct measurements of excitatory synaptic currents in parasol ganglion cells to determine the subunit size, coupling gain between subunits (gain, 0.1), and space constant for electrical coupling in the diffuse bipolar cell networks (λ, 36.4 μm) (Manookin et al., 2018).
evidence: Model parameters derived from authors' previous physiological measurements.

claim: The coupled subunit models showed approach selectivity values of ∼0.5 when the coupling gain was 0.1.
source: The coupled subunit models showed approach selectivity values of ∼0.5 when the coupling gain was 0.1 (On model, 0.56; Off model, 0.46)
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: Models lacking coupling with subunit diameters of 40 µm exhibited much lower approach selectivity than coupled models.
source: but the same models that lacked coupling and with subunit diameters of 40 m exhibited much lower approach selectivity (enlarged subunit model: On model, 0.09; Off model, 0.03).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: Doubling the subunit receptive-field diameters did not reproduce the level of approach selectivity observed in the coupled subunit model or in direct recordings from parasol ganglion cells.
source: In fact, doubling the subunit receptive-field diameters did not reproduce the level of approach selectivity observed in the coupled subunit model or in our direct recordings from parasol ganglion cells (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: Approach bias does not arise primarily from enlarging subunit receptive fields.
source: Thus, approach bias does not arise primarily from enlarging subunit receptive fields.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of coupled vs. enlarged subunit models.

claim: Electrical coupling in the bipolar cell network contributes to approach bias for certain classes of stimuli such as the moving annuli.
source: Thus, the differences in predicted output pattern between these two models suggested that electrical coupling in the bipolar cell network contributes to approach bias for certain classes of stimuli such as the moving annuli (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Inferred from divergent predictions of nonlinear vs. coupled subunit models.

claim: Parasol cells exhibited pronounced asymmetries to approaching and receding annuli.
source: Consistent with the predictions of the coupled subunit model, parasol cells exhibited pronounced asymmetries to approaching and receding annuli.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings to annulus stimuli.

claim: In On parasol cells, approaching bright annuli evoked much larger spike responses than receding annuli of the same contrast.
source: In On parasol cells, approaching bright annuli evoked much larger spike responses than receding annuli of the same contrast—at the highest contrast, approaching motion elicited 85.4 ± 10.9 spikes s–1 versus 7.1 ± 4.3 spikes s–1 for receding motion (contrast, +1.0; mean ± SEM; n = 26 cells; p=8.3 × 10–6; p<2.6 × 10–5 at all contrasts; Wilcoxon signed rank test, here and below).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: In Off parasol cells, approaching motion to strong negative contrasts evoked larger spike responses than receding motion.
source: Likewise, approaching motion to strong negative contrasts in Off parasol cells evoked 148.7 ± 12.8 spikes s–1 versus 55.2 ± 9.4 spikes s–1 for receding motion (contrast, –1.0; mean ± SEM; n = 24 cells; p=2.1 × 10–5; p<3.4 × 10–5 at all contrasts).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: Off smooth monostratified and broad thorny cells lacked consistent approach selectivity to the annulus stimulus.
source: Unlike to the moving textures, Off smooth monostratified and broad thorny cells lacked consistent approach selectivity to the annulus stimulus
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings to annulus stimuli.

claim: Approach selectivity persisted in On smooth monostratified and On and Off parasol cells to the annulus stimulus.
source: but approach selectivity persisted in On smooth monostratified and On and Off parasol cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings to annulus stimuli.

claim: The results aligned well with the predictions of the coupled subunit model, suggesting that electrical coupling or other lateral interactions within the network contributes to approach selectivity in these cells.
source: Besides demonstrating that approach selectivity generalized to a broader range of visual stimuli in the latter three cell types, these results aligned well with the predictions of the coupled subunit model, suggesting that electrical coupling or other lateral interactions within the network contributes to approach selectivity in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from agreement between physiological recordings and coupled subunit model predictions.

claim: The pattern of excitatory synaptic inputs mirrored the observed spiking pattern—excitatory currents were largest for approaching annuli matching the cell's preferred contrast polarity.
source: The pattern of excitatory synaptic inputs mirrored the observed spiking pattern—excitatory currents were largest for approaching annuli matching the cell's preferred contrast polarity—positive contrasts in On cells and negative contrasts in Off cells (compare Figure 6, Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: 100% preferred-contrast approaching annuli evoked excitatory inputs that were much larger than receding annuli in both On and Off parasol cells.
source: For example, 100% preferred-contrast approaching annuli evoked excitatory inputs that were much larger than receding annuli in both On (approaching, 40.4 ± 9.3 pC; receding, 0.7 ± 5.5 pC; n = 16 cells; p=4.4 × 10–4) and Off parasol cells (approaching, 97.5 ± 17.2 pC; receding, 29.0 ± 10.5 pC; n = 19 cells; p=1.3 × 10–4).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: Receding annuli that were of a non-preferred contrast evoked larger responses than approaching annuli of the same contrast.
source: In addition, receding annuli that were of a non-preferred contrast evoked larger responses than approaching annuli of the same contrast.
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The sensitivity to approaching motion observed in the parasol cell spike outputs was present in the excitatory synaptic inputs from diffuse bipolar cells to parasol ganglion cells.
source: These data indicated that the sensitivity to approaching motion observed in the parasol cell spike outputs was present in the excitatory synaptic inputs from diffuse bipolar cells to parasol ganglion cells (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic input to parasol cells showed the opposite pattern to that of excitation.
source: Inhibitory synaptic input to parasol cells showed the opposite pattern to that of excitation.
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: Preferred-contrast receding annuli produced larger inhibitory currents than approaching annuli of the same contrast polarity.
source: Preferred-contrast receding annuli produced larger inhibitory currents than approaching annuli of the same contrast polarity (On: approaching, 89.4 ± 26.9 pC; receding, 127.4 ± 28.6 pC; n = 13 cells; p=0.15; Off: approaching, 64.1 ± 27.7 pC; receding, 114.4 ± 29.3 pC; n = 13 cells; p=1.7 × 10–2).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: The increased selectivity to approaching motion was mediated by a combination of increased synaptic excitation and reduced synaptic inhibition relative to receding motion.
source: This finding indicated that the increased selectivity to approaching motion was mediated by a combination of increased synaptic excitation and reduced synaptic inhibition relative to receding motion
evidence: Inferred from patterns of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.

claim: This pattern of synaptic input amplified the differences in parasol cell responses to approaching and receding motion.
source: this pattern of synaptic input amplified the differences in parasol cell responses to approaching and receding motion.
evidence: Inferred from complementary patterns of excitation and inhibition.

claim: Inhibitory input to parasol cells arises primarily from crossover inhibition.
source: Inhibitory input to parasol cells arises primarily from crossover inhibition (Cafaro and Rieke, 2010; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on parasol cell circuitry.

claim: Crossover inhibition emerges from amacrine cells with opposing contrast polarity—Off-type amacrine cells inhibit On parasol cells and On-type amacrine cells inhibit Off parasol cells.
source: This type of inhibition emerges from amacrine cells with opposing contrast polarity—Off-type amacrine cells inhibit On parasol cells and On-type amacrine cells inhibit Off parasol cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of crossover inhibition circuitry.

claim: Circuits for crossover inhibition can modulate glutamate release from retinal bipolar cells by directly inhibiting their synaptic terminals.
source: In addition to directly inhibiting ganglion cells, circuits for crossover inhibition can modulate glutamate release from retinal bipolar cells by directly inhibiting their synaptic terminals, and this can produce pronounced effects on ganglion cell firing (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Liang and Freed, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on presynaptic inhibition.

claim: Crossover inhibition can manifest in both the direct inhibition onto the ganglion cell and in the excitatory input from bipolar cells.
source: Thus, crossover inhibition can manifest in both the direct inhibition onto the ganglion cell and in the excitatory input from bipolar cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of crossover inhibition mechanisms.

claim: An mGluR6 agonist/antagonist combination (L-APB, 5 µM; LY341495, 7.5 µM) has been shown to silence crossover inhibition while minimizing off-target effects in primate retina.
source: We used an mGluR6 agonist/antagonist combination (L-APB, 5 µM; LY341495, 7.5 µM), which has been shown to silence crossover inhibition while minimizing off-target effects in primate retina (Ala-Laurila et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous pharmacological study.

claim: A comparable pharmacological manipulation was not available for isolating crossover inhibition on On-type ganglion cells.
source: A comparable pharmacological manipulation was not available for isolating crossover inhibition on On-type ganglion cells (Manookin et al., 2018), so we focused on Off parasol cells for these experiments.
evidence: Statement of methodological limitation with supporting citation.

claim: Crossover inhibition can act both presynaptically, by modulating bipolar cell glutamate release, and postsynaptically, by directly inhibiting ganglion cell dendrites.
source: Crossover inhibition can act both presynaptically, by modulating bipolar cell glutamate release, and postsynaptically, by directly inhibiting ganglion cell dendrites (Murphy and Rieke, 2008; Pang et al., 2007; van Wyk et al., 2009; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013; Liang and Freed, 2010; Molnar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on crossover inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Blocking crossover inhibition did not significantly affect the magnitude of evoked excitatory synaptic currents to approaching motion.
source: Blocking crossover inhibition did not significantly affect the magnitude of evoked excitatory synaptic currents to approaching motion
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings before and after pharmacological blockade.

claim: Blocking crossover inhibition increased excitatory currents to receding motion relative to the control condition.
source: but to receding motion, excitatory currents increased following crossover blockade relative to the control condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings before and after pharmacological blockade shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Blocking crossover inhibition reduced approach selectivity relative to the control condition.
source: This subsequently reduced approach selectivity relative to the control condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; n = 6 cells; p=1.6 × 10–2; Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: During receding motion, the amacrine cell responsible for crossover inhibition provided inhibition at presynaptic bipolar terminals, but this presynaptic inhibition was not present during approaching motion.
source: These data indicated that during receding motion, the amacrine cell responsible for crossover inhibition provided inhibition at presynaptic bipolar terminals, but this presynaptic inhibition was not present during approaching motion.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of crossover blockade on excitatory currents during approaching vs. receding motion.

claim: Crossover inhibition was more strongly recruited by receding motion than approaching motion.
source: These excitatory and inhibitory synaptic recordings indicated that crossover inhibition was more strongly recruited by receding motion than approaching motion.
evidence: Inferred from patterns of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.

claim: Crossover inhibition enhanced approach motion selectivity by suppressing excitatory synaptic release and directly inhibiting ganglion cell dendrites during receding motion.
source: Thus, crossover inhibition enhanced approach motion selectivity by suppressing excitatory synaptic release and directly inhibiting ganglion cell dendrites during receding motion.
evidence: Inferred from effects of crossover blockade on excitatory and inhibitory currents.

claim: Excitatory synaptic input was larger for approaching motion than receding motion with crossover inhibition blocked.
source: Despite the apparent contribution of crossover inhibition to approach motion selectivity, excitatory synaptic input was larger for approaching motion than receding motion with crossover inhibition blocked.
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with crossover inhibition blocked.

claim: The observed bias for approaching motion was present in both the bipolar cell and amacrine cell circuitries and was amplified by interactions between these circuit elements.
source: This indicated that the observed bias for approaching motion was present in both the bipolar cell and amacrine cell circuitries and was amplified by interactions between these circuit elements.
evidence: Inferred from persistence of approach bias after crossover blockade and differential effects on excitation and inhibition.

claim: Parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells consistently showed larger responses to approaching textures and annuli relative to receding stimuli of the same type.
source: We compared the responses of several primate ganglion cell types to approaching and receding motion. We found that parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells consistently showed larger responses to approaching textures and annuli relative to receding stimuli of the same type (Figure 1, Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings shown in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: The asymmetrical response patterns of parasol and smooth monostratified cells to approaching and receding motion arises from the concerted activity of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to these ganglion cells.
source: We further demonstrated that the asymmetrical response patterns of these cells to approaching and receding motion arises from the concerted activity of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to these ganglion cells (Figure 5, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figures 5, 7, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approach selectivity was weak or absent from several On-Off type cells indicating that it was not a general property of primate ganglion cells.
source: Further, approach selectivity was weak or absent from several On-Off type cells indicating that it was not a general property of primate ganglion cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings from multiple cell types.

claim: Canonical receptive-field models have been used to describe the visual properties of many ganglion cell types including parasol cells.
source: Canonical receptive-field models have been used to describe the visual properties of many ganglion cell types including parasol cells (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Canonical receptive-field models have been used to describe the visual properties of smooth monostratified cells.
source: Canonical receptive-field models have been used to describe the visual properties of many ganglion cell types including parasol cells (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002) and smooth monostratified cells (Crook et al., 2008; Petrusca et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Canonical receptive-field models can accurately predict neural responses to briefly presented stimuli.
source: These models can accurately predict neural responses to a small subset of potential visual inputs such as briefly presented stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated through model predictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Canonical receptive-field models can accurately predict neural responses to spatiotemporally uncorrelated noise.
source: These models can accurately predict neural responses to a small subset of potential visual inputs such as briefly presented stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or spatiotemporally uncorrelated noise (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study.

claim: Canonical receptive-field models perform poorly at predicting responses to stimuli containing spatiotemporal correlations.
source: but they perform poorly at predicting responses to stimuli containing spatiotemporal correlations (Manookin et al., 2018; Kuo et al., 2016), including naturalistic stimuli (Heitman et al., 2016; Turner and Rieke, 2016; Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing model failures.

claim: These failures occur because retinal circuits contain many nonlinearities that are not considered in classical receptive field models.
source: These failures occur because retinal circuits contain many nonlinearities that are not considered in classical receptive field models.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of retinal circuit properties.

claim: The traditional linear-nonlinear spatiotemporal model failed to accurately predict the strong asymmetries observed to approaching and receding motion.
source: Indeed, the traditional linear-nonlinear spatiotemporal model failed to accurately predict the strong asymmetries observed to approaching and receding motion (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of model predictions to physiological data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In vertebrates, the principal retinal nonlinearities arise at the level of bipolar cell glutamate release.
source: In vertebrates, the principal retinal nonlinearities arise at the level of bipolar cell glutamate release (Demb et al., 2001; Demb et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on bipolar cell physiology.

claim: Additional nonlinearities are produced by electrical coupling between bipolar cells.
source: Additional nonlinearities are produced by electrical coupling between bipolar cells (Kuo et al., 2016; Manookin et al., 2018; Trenholm et al., 2013; Hoggarth et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on electrical coupling.

claim: Additional nonlinearities are produced by inhibitory amacrine cells.
source: and by inhibitory amacrine cells (Kim and Kerschensteiner, 2017; Dong and Werblin, 1998; de Vries et al., 2011; Baccus et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on amacrine cell function.

claim: A recent study revealed strong nonlinearities in the interactions between different dendritic branches of smooth monostratified ganglion cells.
source: Further, a recent study revealed strong nonlinearities in the interactions between different dendritic branches of smooth monostratified ganglion cells, providing an additional level of nonlinear interactions after the bipolar cell nonlinearities (Rhoades et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study on dendritic nonlinearities.

claim: Retinal nonlinearities form the basis for extracting (or rejecting) specific features from visual inputs.
source: Besides frustrating attempts by researchers to produce accurate computational models of retinal processing, these nonlinearities form the basis for extracting (or rejecting) specific features from visual inputs.
evidence: Based on established understanding of nonlinear processing in neural circuits.

claim: Amacrine cell input allows the ∼15 bipolar cell types to differentially affect the ∼30–40 ganglion cell pathways.
source: For example, amacrine cell input allows the ∼15 bipolar cell types to differentially affect the ∼30–40 ganglion cell pathways (Asari and Meister, 2012; Asari and Meister, 2014; Masland, 2012; Wässle, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on retinal circuit organization.

claim: Interactions between bipolar and amacrine cells contribute to spatial selectivity.
source: Further, these interactions contribute to spatial selectivity (Greschner et al., 2016; Olveczky et al., 2003; Cook and McReynolds, 1998; Taylor, 1999; Flores-Herr et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on spatial processing.

claim: Interactions between bipolar and amacrine cells contribute to short-term plasticity.
source: and short-term plasticity (Naecker, 2018; Kastner and Baccus, 2011; Kastner and Baccus, 2013; Appleby and Manookin, 2019; Kastner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on adaptation and plasticity.

claim: Crossover inhibition arises via interactions between the On and Off visual pathways.
source: The prominent type of inhibitory input at play in approach motion selectivity, crossover inhibition, arises via interactions between the On and Off visual pathways.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of crossover inhibition circuitry.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved across several vertebrate species including fish.
source: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved across several vertebrate species including fish (Rosa et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to study in fish.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved in salamanders.
source: salamanders (Pang et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to study in salamanders.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved in guinea pigs.
source: guinea pigs (Liang and Freed, 2010; Manookin et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in guinea pigs.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved in rodents.
source: rodents (Münch et al., 2009; van Wyk et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in rodents.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved in rabbits.
source: rabbits (Molnar et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to study in rabbits.

claim: The circuit motif for crossover inhibition has been conserved in primates.
source: and primates (Cafaro and Rieke, 2010; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in primates.

claim: Crossover inhibition contributes to a variety of visual functions.
source: and it contributes to a variety of visual functions (reviewed in Werblin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: Crossover inhibition amplifies the asymmetrical responses of primate ganglion cells to approaching and receding motion by providing inhibition both at the level of the diffuse bipolar cell terminals and at the level of the ganglion cell dendrites.
source: Here, we demonstrate that crossover inhibition amplifies the asymmetrical responses of primate ganglion cells to approaching and receding motion by providing inhibition both at the level of the diffuse bipolar cell terminals and at the level of the ganglion cell dendrites (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Münch et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with crossover blockade shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Electrical coupling between neighboring bipolar cells enhances responses to visual inputs containing spatiotemporal correlations.
source: Electrical coupling between neighboring bipolar cells enhances responses to visual inputs containing spatiotemporal correlations and endows certain ganglion cells with generalized motion selectivity (Kuo et al., 2016; Manookin et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on electrical coupling and motion processing.

claim: Electrical coupling enhances direction selectivity in some ganglion cells.
source: and enhanced direction selectivity in others (Hoggarth et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on direction selectivity.

claim: The effects of electrical synaptic transmission varies with the type of motion—potentiation occurs during approaching motion and was absent during receding motion.
source: Our results here suggest that the effects of electrical synaptic transmission varies with the type of motion—potentiation occurs during approaching motion and was absent during receding motion (Figure 5, Appendix 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling results shown in Figure 5 and Appendix 1.

claim: The prevalence of electrical synapses in the retina was partly an adaptation, early in vertebrate evolution, for processing the spatiotemporal correlations that are so common in visual environments.
source: Perhaps, the prevalence of these synapses in the retina was partly an adaptation, early in vertebrate evolution, for processing the spatiotemporal correlations that are so common in visual environments (Völgyi et al., 2013; Field, 1987), including those generated during an animal's own motion through the environment (Figure 1, Figure 4; Clifford et al., 1999; Schrater et al., 2001; Dong and Atick, 1995).
evidence: Speculative statement about evolutionary adaptation with supporting citations.

claim: In rodent retina, approach selectivity is found only in a single ganglion cell class—the Off Alpha ganglion cell and is absent from several other types.
source: In rodent retina, approach selectivity is found only in a single ganglion cell class—the Off Alpha ganglion cell and is absent from several other types (Münch et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study in rodents.

claim: Approach selectivity is more ubiquitous in the primate retina, manifesting in parasol, smooth monostratified, and broad thorny ganglion cells to varying degrees.
source: We found approach selectivity to be more ubiquitous in the primate retina, manifesting in parasol, smooth monostratified, and broad thorny ganglion cells to varying degrees (Figure 1, Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated through spike recordings shown in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: The variation in approach selectivity across species may reflect the distinct ethological demands on these species.
source: This variation may reflect the distinct ethological demands on these species.
evidence: Speculative statement about functional significance.

claim: The need to quickly detect approaching dark objects, such as overhead predators would be necessary for survival in prey species like mice.
source: For example, the need to quickly detect approaching dark objects, such as overhead predators would be necessary for survival in prey species like mice (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative statement about functional significance with supporting citation.

claim: Expression of approach selectivity in an Off-type ganglion cell would allow vital computations to occur early in the visual pathway.
source: Thus, expression of approach selectivity in an Off-type ganglion cell would allow these vital computations to occur early in the visual pathway.
evidence: Speculative statement about functional significance.

claim: The arboreal habitats of early primates increased the need to quickly and accurately perform visually guided movements with the arms and hands.
source: Likewise, the arboreal habitats of early primates increased the need to quickly and accurately perform visually guided movements with the arms and hands and led to the expansion of areas in the parietal cortex responsible for these tasks (Goodale and Milner, 1992).
evidence: Speculative statement about evolutionary pressures with supporting citation.

claim: Arboreal habitats may have produced a need for light/dark symmetry in detecting approaching motion as well as self-motion through the environment.
source: These habitats may have also produced a need for light/dark symmetry in detecting approaching motion as well as self-motion through the environment (Clifford et al., 1999; Schrater et al., 2001).
evidence: Speculative statement about evolutionary pressures with supporting citations.

claim: The selectivity of macaque ganglion cell types to approaching motion should be distinguished from the looming-sensitive neurons found in retinorecepient brain regions.
source: The selectivity of these macaque ganglion cell types to approaching motion should be distinguished from the looming-sensitive neurons found in retinorecepient brain regions.
evidence: Statement distinguishing current findings from related phenomena.

claim: Looming-sensitive neurons in the optic tectum of pigeons respond when an object moves toward the animal, but do not respond when the animal moves toward the object.
source: For example, looming-sensitive neurons in the optic tectum of pigeons respond when an object moves toward the animal, but do not respond when the animal moves toward the object (Sun and Frost, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study in pigeons.

claim: The ganglion cells tested would not be able to distinguish self-motion and object motion.
source: The ganglion cells that we tested would not be able to distinguish self-motion and object motion in this way.
evidence: Inferred from stimulus properties and response characteristics.

claim: The approach motion selectivity observed would be an initial step in a series of computations culminating in the detection of approaching objects.
source: Instead, the approach motion selectivity that we observed would be an initial step in a series of computations culminating in the detection of approaching objects.
evidence: Speculative statement about functional role in visual processing hierarchy.

claim: The same circuit nonlinearities that enhanced selectivity to approaching motion also produced ambiguities between the direction (approaching/receding) and contrast (light/dark) of moving objects.
source: Indeed, the same circuit nonlinearities that enhanced selectivity to approaching motion also produced ambiguities between the direction (approaching/receding) and contrast (light/dark) of moving objects.
evidence: Inferred from response patterns showing contrast-dependent direction preferences.

claim: Downstream visual circuits receiving input from parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells would require input from other retinal pathways to resolve ambiguities between direction and contrast.
source: This result indicates that downstream visual circuits receiving input from parasol and smooth monostratified ganglion cells would also require input from other retinal pathways to resolve these ambiguities.
evidence: Inferred from observed ambiguities in ganglion cell responses.

claim: Downstream circuits might obtain a more faithful readout of the reflectance of a moving object from the concerted activity of midget ganglion cells.
source: For example, downstream circuits might obtain a more faithful readout of the reflectance of a moving object from the concerted activity of midget ganglion cells and then, with the aid of this information, determine whether the object were approaching or receding.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential downstream processing mechanisms.

claim: Future studies will be needed to determine how and where in the visual stream ambiguities between direction and contrast are resolved.
source: However, future studies will be needed to determine how and where in the visual stream such ambiguities are resolved.
evidence: Statement of future research directions.

claim: Experiments were performed in an in vitro, pigment-epithelium attached preparation of the macaque monkey retina.
source: Experiments were performed in an in vitro, pigment-epithelium attached preparation of the macaque monkey retina (Manookin et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of experimental methods with supporting citation.

claim: Eyes were dissected from terminally anesthetized macaque monkeys of either sex obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the National Primate Research Center at the University of Washington.
source: Eyes were dissected from terminally anesthetized macaque monkeys of either sex (Macaca fascicularis, mulatta, and nemestrina) obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the National Primate Research Center at the University of Washington.
evidence: Description of tissue source and experimental methods.

claim: All procedures were approved by the University of Washington Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were approved by the University of Washington Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: The retina was continuously superfused with warmed (32–35°C) Ames' medium at ∼6–8 mL min–1.
source: The retina was continuously superfused with warmed (32–35°C) Ames' medium (Sigma) at ∼6–8 mL min–1.
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Recordings were performed from macular, mid-peripheral, or peripheral retina (2–8 mm, 10–30° foveal eccentricity).
source: Recordings were performed from macular, mid-peripheral, or peripheral retina (2–8 mm, 10–30° foveal eccentricity).
evidence: Description of recording locations.
